slides.title: the dream in one sentence
slides.notes: The synthesis of twenty years of laboratory-automation work: the robot, the communication standard, the data formats, the ontologies, the consortium. Each is a fragment; this is the machine they add up to.

blocks.text: A self-driving enzyme-engineering laboratory whose entire memory is a **knowledge graph**.
No lab notebook. No human transcription. No result whose provenance cannot be walked.
the machines that produce the data describe it themselves, so the metadata is right by construction rather than by discipline.

slides.title: the loop, closed
slides.notes: Design-Build-Test-Learn is the standard framing of protein engineering. The dream is that no human hand is needed to carry results from one step to the next — and that the LEARN step reads a graph, not a pile of spreadsheets.

items: **design** — ML-assisted enzyme design, already published practice in the group
**build + test** — LARA: growth, expression, lysis, purification, assay — one robotic line
**learn** — every result lands *already semantically described*, linked to ChEBI, Rhea, UniProt
and the loop turns again — overnight, unattended, *documented by construction*

slides.title: every number can testify
slides.notes: Provenance as a property of infrastructure rather than a virtue of people. The chain here is the real chain of an automated screening platform. In the dream, this walk is one click, for every number ever produced.

blocks.text: click any measurement and walk **all the way back**
reproducibility stops being a virtue and becomes a **property of the infrastructure**.

slides.title: one graph, three worlds
slides.notes: The join that makes it more than a lab database: local experiments, the world's curated knowledge, and the literature share identifiers, so evidence flows across them. This is exactly the layer the tacat project exercised.

blocks.text: the lab
every screen, every mutant, every failure — captured by the machines that ran them
the world
ChEBI, Rhea, UniProt — the curated public memory of biochemistry
joined by **shared identifiers**, queried as one.
ask: *which enzyme converts this substrate, under these conditions, on what evidence?* — and the answer cites experiments, not opinions.

slides.title: the dark matter
slides.notes: The quiet revolution hidden inside FAIR. Most screening results are negative and are lost — so every lab re-explores dead sequence space. A graph that keeps failures makes the map of what does NOT work as available as what does.

blocks.text: most of what a screen produces is **failure** — and today, failure is thrown away.
every lab re-explores sequence space that another lab already knows is dead.
in the dream, the failures are kept — and *the map of what does not work* becomes as queryable as the successes.
this is what FAIR data is actually for. not compliance — collective memory.

slides.title: what becomes findable
slides.notes: The payoff slide — the dream cashed out as capabilities. FIND: discovery on demand. SEE: total provenance. KNOW: the landscape itself, with the holes visible and plannable.

blocks.text: find
enzymes **on demand** — a transaminase for *this* substrate becomes a query, then a campaign, not a three-year project
see
the **complete causal chain** behind every number — nothing untraceable, nothing irreproducible
know

the sequence–function landscape of enzyme families as a **navigable object** — each claim backed by a walkable experiment, each hole in knowledge visible, and plannable as the next automated campaign.

slides.title: from molecule to process
slides.notes: NFDI4Cat's own slogan. The silos named here are the consortium's founding complaint: quantum chemistry, molecular biology and process engineering cannot read each other's data. One graph crossing them is the institutional half of the dream.

blocks.text: today these are **mutually unintelligible subfields** — incompatible formats, no shared vocabulary, data locked in group-local spreadsheets.
in the dream they are one graph, and a question can *cross the silos*.

slides.title: open by construction
slides.notes: The political layer, and it is not decoration — the open-source commitment is stated openly in this field. Commodity robots, free software, shared memory — the dream is not a proprietary self-driving lab at a chemical major.

blocks.text: the dream is **not** a proprietary self-driving lab behind a corporate firewall.

items: the software is free — GPL and MIT, maintained in the open
the standards are open — SiLA2, RDF, SPARQL, JSON-LD
the knowledge is shared — FAIR by default

blocks.text: a **small academic lab** gets the same machine.

slides.title: two ends of one spectrum
slides.notes: Deliberately simplified — neither column is strictly true. Open-world logic already says unknown rather than false, and a model at temperature zero is a deterministic function. But the FAILURE MODES really are mirror images, and that is the part worth keeping.

blocks.text: logic — crystal
truth survives composition. a chain of a million inferences loses nothing.
the price: the world must be curated into symbols first, and one wrong symbol poisons everything downstream — silently, permanently.
ML — weather
touches the raw world without asking permission — noisy spectra, missing labels, patterns nobody formalised.
the price: nothing composes. chain two outputs and errors do not add, they breed. and it cannot decline.
logic fails at the **entrance** — getting the world in. ML fails at the **exit** — getting trust out.

slides.title: the same object, twice
slides.notes: The metaphor, stated once so the rest of the deck can lean on it. Left: every cell is in or out, the boundary is visible, and you can point at it. Right: a value everywhere, no boundary anywhere, nothing to point at. Neither is wrong — they answer different questions.

blocks.text: pixels — logic
a decision you can point at, and defend.
gradient — ML
a value everywhere, and nowhere to draw the line.

slides.title: equivalence is not similarity
slides.notes: The deepest coordinate, and the one that breaks joins silently. Transitivity is what licenses substitution, and substitution is what proofs, queries and joins are made of. Similarity has no transitivity, therefore no substitution, therefore cannot carry a ledger.

blocks.text: similarity **ranks**. equivalence licenses **replacement**.

and every real equivalence is manufactured — by declaring which differences do not count. *same molecule, up to protonation.* the ChEBI join failed because two such declarations collided, and neither was written down.

slides.title: the space
slides.notes: The arithmetic that makes the architecture necessary. Four saturated positions is already 160,000 variants; five is 3.2 million. Multiply by substrates and conditions. The robot is fast and it does not matter — the space wins by five orders of magnitude.

items.label: points the robot will ever visit

blocks.text: variants × substrates × conditions — against a working lifetime of screening
you will see **one ten-thousandth of one percent**.
so choosing where to look is not a preliminary to the science. it *is* the science.

slides.title: finding is hard, checking is cheap
slides.notes: The asymmetry the whole split rests on. Not a compromise between paradigms — each technology placed on the side its cost profile suits. Say the veto line and stop; it is the thesis of the deck.

blocks.text: the space of candidate answers is enormous. validating **one** candidate is bounded work.
ML has the **ideas**. logic has the **veto**.

the inexact, cheap, creative technology goes on the expensive side; the exact one goes where exactness is affordable — and whatever sits in the veto seat must be *auditable*, re-runnable by someone who does not trust it.

slides.title: search has two halves
slides.notes: And the order matters: you cannot rank 10^11 candidates and then discard most of them, so feasibility acts as a GENERATOR defining the space sampled from, not a sieve applied afterwards. The last row is the equivalence/similarity distinction one level up.

head: 1 · feasible?
2 · how promising?
rows: **yes** — *not in inventory, no supplier under six weeks*

blocks.text: feasibility runs **first**, and as a *generator* — it defines the space that is sampled, rather than sieving a list already produced.

slides.title: the trap
slides.notes: Where the vision most easily fails, and it is subtle. Will-it-fold FEELS like a fact. It is a prediction. Put it in the filter and a prediction has taken the veto seat — and it is self-confirming, because what you exclude you never test, so the model is never contradicted there.

head: tier
example
genuinely binary?
rows: in stock · codon valid · **already tested** · assay covers it
will it fold? will it express? soluble at 40 °C?

blocks.text: exclude what the model doubts, never test it, never contradict it — **the blind spot never heals.**

wrongly excluded is silent and permanent; wrongly included costs one well and corrects itself. so **be strict where the constraint is a fact, generous where it is a prediction** — demote, never delete.

slides.title: two ways to search
slides.notes: The correction to the loop slide that follows. BOTH are sound — everything either one returns is genuinely feasible. They differ in completeness, and completeness is what buys you the ability to say NO. Point at the pale cells: those are real solutions that were never proposed, and nothing in the right-hand picture knows they are missing.

blocks.text: both are **sound** — everything either one returns is genuinely feasible. only the left is **complete**.
so the right can prove something **exists**. it can never prove that **nothing does**.

slides.title: the border crossing
slides.notes: The resolution, and why automation is load-bearing rather than convenient. Logic can only check consistency with what is already known; for anything genuinely new the only valid check is the experiment. Automation makes that check cheap enough to run at the speed the first two tiers generate candidates.

slides.title: and it may refuse
slides.notes: The property most systems omit, and the one that decides whether any of this is usable in a laboratory. A lab ACTS on answers — a plausible wrong answer does not merely mislead a reader, it sends a machine to run the wrong plate for a week.

items: the query is shown **in prose** before it runs — the only check on intent that exists
the answer arrives with its **derivation**, re-runnable by someone who does not trust the system
an empty answer is **diagnosed, never returned bare** — which clause killed it, and what would return something
similarity is available but **never silently promoted to identity**
and the system may say: *I could not turn your question into a query I can justify*

blocks.text: a system that **fails well** is worth more than one that always answers.

slides.notes: Close on the consortium's own phrase, completed by the dream: nothing lost on the way — no data, no failure, no provenance. That is the whole adventure in one line.
